llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan – “Stock‐price shocks and corporate decision-making during the late-1990s tech bubble”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Panel Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) with firm and calendar-quarter fixed effects, complemented by an event-study DID for robustness.

Why IV?  
•  Stock prices are jointly determined with investment/financing (reverse causality).  
•  The tech bubble generated large, sentiment-driven price movements that are plausibly orthogonal to contemporaneous fundamentals.  
•  We can proxy this ‘non-fundamental’ component with instruments derived from peer firms’ returns, which are highly correlated with the firm’s own price but do not enter its investment opportunity set except through the price.

Event-study DID (pre/post March-2000 crash, high- vs low-run-up firms) provides a transparent, assumption-light complement and allows visual inspection of parallel trends.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_it  = log(stock price)_it   (levels)  OR  M/B_it (market-to-book).  
For robustness we scale by lagged assets (price × shares ÷ assets).

Instrument (Z_it)  
“Peer sentiment return” ≡ value-weighted return of all other firms in the same 3-digit SIC tech industry in quarter t, excluding firm i:

Z_it = Σ_{j≠i} w_{jt}·R_{jt}

Control group / counterfactual  
Firms experiencing smaller peer-sentiment shocks in the same calendar quarter provide the within-time cross-sectional counterfactual (achieved through quarter FEs).

Event-study version  
•  Event date: 2000q1–q2 crash (NASDAQ peak 10 Mar 2000).  
•  Treated = top tercile of abnormal pre-crash price run-up (1998q1–1999q4 cumulative return net of industry fundamentals).  
•  Control = bottom tercile.  
•  Pre-period: 1995q1–1999q4; Post-period: 2000q2–2003q4.

No RDD running variable is used.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance – Peer returns co-move strongly with the firm’s own price because investors extrapolate industry sentiment. Likely satisfied in a bubble (testable via first-stage F-stat).

A2. Exclusion restriction – Conditional on firm & quarter FEs and controls (industry fundamentals, demand shocks, macro variables), peer-sentiment returns affect the firm’s investment/financing only through the firm’s own stock price. Plausible because most projects are idiosyncratic, yet we must defend against common demand shocks (see Threats).

A3. Independence – After controlling, peer returns are as-good-as random with respect to the firm’s idiosyncratic investment opportunity set. The sharp, sentiment-driven nature of the bubble helps.

A4. Stable unit treatment value – One firm’s treatment does not mechanically alter another’s outcome beyond what is captured by common quarter shocks (quarter FEs).

Event-study additional assumption: parallel pre-crash trends in investment between high- and low-run-up firms (visually testable).

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Common demand/technology shocks could drive both peer returns and the firm’s investment (violates exclusion).  
Mitigation:  
•  Control for contemporaneous industry-level fundamentals (avg sales growth, R&D intensity).  
•  Include industry×quarter fixed effects in robustness checks.  
•  Use lagged peer returns as an alternative instrument to purge contemporaneous demand components.

T2. Mechanical balance-sheet effects (a rising price increases collateral or reduces leverage, directly relaxing financing constraints rather than “sentiment”). That is part of the causal chain we wish to estimate, so not a violation. But we must separate financing and real-investment channels.  
Mitigation: Estimate investment and financing equations separately; add internal-cash-flow and collateral controls to see if coefficients attenuate.

T3. Measurement error in stock prices (bid-ask bounce, stock splits).  
Mitigation:  
•  Use split-adjusted, end-of-quarter prices.  
•  Winsorise top/bottom 1 %.  
•  Verify robustness with market-capitalisation and Tobin’s q measures.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --- 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast high-dim FE + IV
library(ggplot2)

# --- 1. Load ----------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("tech_firm_quarter.csv")   # assumes panel: firm_id, fqtr (YYYYQ), etc.

# --- 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------------
# Date helpers
dt[, year  := as.integer(substr(fqtr, 1, 4))]
dt[, qtr   := as.integer(substr(fqtr, 6, 6))]

# Price variables
dt[, logP        := log(adj_close)]              # adj_close is split-adjusted
dt[, mb_ratio    := mkt_cap / book_equity]

# Investment & financing
dt[, inv_rate    := capex / shift(total_assets, type="lag", n=1)]
dt[, equity_iss  := (delta_common_shares * adj_close) / shift(total_assets, 1)]
dt[, debt_iss    := (long_term_debt - shift(long_term_debt, 1)) / shift(total_assets,1)]

# Peer-sentiment instrument
# Compute industry-quarter return excluding own firm
dt[, peer_ret := NA_real_]
for (t in unique(dt$fqtr)){
  tmp <- dt[fqtr == t]
  setkey(tmp, sic3)               # 3-digit SIC within tech
  tmp[, ind_ret := weighted.mean(ret, mkt_cap, na.rm=TRUE), by=sic3]
  tmp[, peer_ret := (ind_ret*mkt_cap_tot - ret*mkt_cap) / (mkt_cap_tot - mkt_cap),
      by=sic3,
      .SDcols=c("ret","mkt_cap","ind_ret")]
  dt[fqtr == t, peer_ret := tmp$peer_ret]
}

# --- 3. Main 2SLS specification --------------------------------------------
# Investment equation
iv_inv <- feols(inv_rate ~ cfoper/lag_assets + controls | firm_id + fqtr | 
                logP ~ peer_ret, data=dt, cluster = "firm_id")
summary(iv_inv)

# Financing equation (equity issuance)
iv_eq  <- feols(equity_iss ~ controls | firm_id + fqtr | logP ~ peer_ret,
                data=dt, cluster="firm_id")

# --- 4. Robustness: include industry×time FE -------------------------------
iv_inv_ind <- feols(inv_rate ~ cfoper/lag_assets + 
                    fe(industry_qtr) | firm_id + fqtr | logP ~ peer_ret,
                    data=dt, cluster="firm_id")

# --- 5. Event-study DID plot -----------------------------------------------
# Define treatment terciles
dt[, cum_runup := prod(1+ret[fqtr %between% c("1998Q1","1999Q4")]) - 1, by=firm_id]
dt[, treat_grp := cut(cum_runup,
               breaks=quantile(cum_runup, probs=c(0,1/3,2/3,1), na.rm=TRUE),
               labels=c("Low","Mid","High"), include.lowest=TRUE)]
# Event-time
dt[, event_time := (year - 2000)*4 + (qtr - 2)]   # 0 = 2000Q2
ests <- feols(inv_rate ~ i(event_time, treat_grp=="High", ref=-1) |
              firm_id + fqtr, data=dt[event_time %between% c(-12,12)],
              cluster="firm_id")
iplot(ests)

```
(controls can include firm size, leverage, cash flow, sales growth, R&D, etc.)

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (Stein 1996 feedback model) predicts that higher (possibly over-valued) stock prices relax financing constraints and make equity issuance cheaper, leading to:

•  Positive effect on equity issuance: a 1 sd (≈30 %) increase in log price ⇒ +2–3 p.p. of assets in net equity issued per quarter.  
•  Positive but smaller effect on real investment: same shock ⇒ +0.4–0.6 p.p. of assets in cap-ex (about a 15–25 % increase over mean tech cap-ex).

During the crash the signs reverse: large negative price shocks should sharply curtail equity issuance first, then investment with a lag.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV method)
C1. Relevance (F-stat > 10) …………………… 1  
C2. Exclusion (no direct path) ………………… 0.5 (plausible but not certain)  
C3. Independence / as-good-as-random ……… 0.5  
C4. Correct functional form / linearity ……… 1  
C5. No systematic measurement error ……… 1  

Total ≈ 4/5. The main weakness is the exclusion/independence of the peer-return instrument, which we address through richer fixed effects, controls, and multiple robustness checks.
